## Statistical Analysis

All statistical analyses were conducted using Bayesian multilevel modeling. The primary implementation used the Region-Based Analysis (RBA) program [@chen2019HandlingMultiplicityNeuroimaging] from the AFNI software suite, which provides a neuroimaging-optimized interface for Bayesian hierarchical models. RBA employs Bayesian inference through the brms package [@burkner2017BrmsPackageBayesian] and the Stan probabilistic programming language, but provides convenient wrappers for handling the nested structure of neuroimaging data (regions nested within subjects).

Bayesian multilevel modeling offers several advantages over traditional frequentist approaches for this type of analysis. First, it naturally handles the hierarchical structure of the data, allowing us to model both within-subject and between-subject variability while appropriately accounting for the non-independence of observations. Second, it provides full posterior distributions for all parameters, allowing us to quantify uncertainty and make probabilistic statements about effect sizes. Third, it enables partial pooling, where region-specific estimates "borrow strength" from the overall pattern across regions, leading to more stable estimates especially for regions with high variability or outliers. Fourth, it provides a principled approach to multiple comparisons through the hierarchical model structure, avoiding the need for ad-hoc corrections that can be overly conservative.


###  Distribution of variables of interest

To examine potential differences in inter-trial phase coherence (ITPC) across experimental conditions, we conducted a Bayesian multilevel analysis using the brms package (Bürkner, 2017) in R ( R version `4.5.1` and brms version `2.22`). 
 <!-- This preliminary analysis was performed to determine whether conditions could be appropriately combined in subsequent modeling. -->

 First part we used data from the PRE condition

We looked into simple model where and how much  ASSR change ITPC.
My assumption is that the  effect of  sound  stimulation will be dependent both from the Subject and roi (@barr2013RandomEffectsStructure argues for maximal structure of model being conservative)
$$  ITPC \sim  1+  S + (1+ S|ROI) + (1 + S|Subject)$$

Similarly we do use similar structure for parameters of the slope - exponent and offset

$$ exponent \sim 1 + S  + (1 + S|ROI) + (1 + S|Subject)$$

$$ offset \sim 1 + S  + (1 + S|ROI) + (1 + S|Subject)$$

We decided to fit sigma  in the models as well to capture the uncertainty more precisely -  Different subjects may not only differ in their mean responses but also in their consistency and ifferent ROIs might have different signal-to-noise ratios.

#### Main Analysis

A hierarchical Bayesian model was implemented using the brms package to assess the relationship between ITPC and spectral exponent. The model was specified as:

$$
itpc \sim 1 + exponent_z + (1 + exponent_z | roi) + (1 + exponent_z | subject)
$$
This formula represents ITPC as a function of the standardized spectral exponent (exponent_z), while accounting for random intercepts and slopes for both brain regions (roi) and subjects. We employed Student's t-distribution as the likelihood function to accommodate potential outliers in the data. The model was fitted using Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling with 4 chains, 4000 iterations per chain, and a 1000-iteration warm-up period. To improve convergence, we set the adapt_delta parameter to 0.95.


To interpret region-specific effects, we extracted random effects for each ROI using the extract_region_effects function. This allowed us to calculate:

Base ITPC values (intercept) for each brain region
The effect of spectral exponent on ITPC in each region
Posterior probabilities (P+) indicating the likelihood of positive effects
95% credible intervals for parameter estimates

We calculated predicted ITPC values at different levels of the spectral exponent (±1 standard deviation from the mean) to quantify effect sizes across regions. Brain regions were then ranked based on both the magnitude of the spectral exponent effect and the posterior probability of the effect being positive or negative. Results were visualized using brain plots to illustrate the spatial distribution of effects.


#### ITPC Comparison Between Experimental Conditions including tDCS


<!-- The dataset included ITPC measurements from multiple subjects across different regions of interest (ROIs), with experimental manipulations involving transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) and sham conditions, measured at both pre-stimulation and post-stimulation timepoints. Data were collected using the Destrieux atlas parcellation for ROI definition. -->

We constructed a hierarchical Bayesian model with ITPC as the dependent variable. Fixed effects included the main effects of measurement time point (P: pre vs. post), stimulation type (T: tDCS vs. sham), and their interaction (P×T). The model incorporated subject-specific and ROI-specific random intercepts and slopes for all fixed effects, allowing for individual variation in both baseline ITPC values and responses to the experimental manipulations.
The model specification was:

$$itpc \sim ~  1 + P*T + (1 + P*T | roi) + (1 + P*T | subject)$$

We used a Student's t-distribution as the likelihood function to accommodate potential outliers in the data. The model was fitted using four Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) chains with 4,000 iterations each (including 1,000 warmup iterations), resulting in 12,000 post-warmup samples for posterior inference. To improve convergence, we set the adapt_delta parameter to 0.95.

For hypothesis testing, we examined the posterior distributions of the regression coefficients, focusing on the main effects of time point and stimulation type, as well as their interaction. We calculated probability values (P+) for each ROI-specific parameter, representing the probability of a positive effect when the mean was positive, or a negative effect when the mean was negative. Effects were considered to show strong evidence when P+ exceeded 0.95 (strong evidence for a positive effect) or fell below 0.05 (strong evidence for a negative effect).

## Methods

- The PSD of the spectrum were computed for 1 s second pre-stimulus period and stimulation period for each trial (and averaged later) and for each region.  
  The slope and exponent were computed using specparam toolbox [3].

- ITPC was computed, the value averaged in the intervals [−500, −200] ms for prestimuli and [400, 700] ms after sound onset for each of the regions using the wavelet approach described in [2].

- The influence of the stimulus and the exponent on the ITPC were tested by modelling the different relationships with an integrative Bayesian Multilevel Model [1].

- This method allows for better integration of the spatial information and control of multiplicity avoiding information loss of univariate approach followed by the correction for multiple testing.

- Effect estimation and region-level inferences are based on posterior distributions of group differences.

**Following models were tested:**

1.
2. ITPC ~ Exponent + Stimulus  
3. Exponent ~ Stimulus  
4. Offset ~ Stimulus  
5. For investigation of the relationship we fit the model  
   `ITPC : stim Exponent : stim + (1 + Exponent : stim|ROI) + (1 + Exponent : stim|Subject)`  
   using *z*-scored Exponent. The model was fitted using the **brms** package and *rstan*.


# Main Model Specification

We fitted separate models to test: (1) the effect of auditory 
stimulation on ITPC, (2) the effect of tDCS on ITPC and spectral 
parameters, and (3) the relationship between spectral exponent and 
ITPC.

For the primary analysis examining the exponent-ITPC relationship, 
we specified:

ITPC_stim ~ 1 + exponent_z + (1 + exponent_z | subject) + (1 | ROI)

where exponent_z represents the within-subject standardized spectral 
exponent, and random effects account for both subject-specific 
variation in baseline ITPC and in the exponent-ITPC relationship, 
as well as ROI-specific baseline differences. This specification 
allows the exponent-ITPC relationship to vary across subjects while 
incorporating partial pooling across ROIs.

We employed a Student's t-distribution likelihood (df = 3) to 
accommodate potential outliers. All models were fitted using 4 MCMC 
chains with 4,000 iterations each (1,000 warmup), with adapt_delta 
set to 0.95 to ensure adequate exploration of the posterior 
distribution.

# Results

Inference and Multiple Comparisons

For each ROI, we extracted posterior distributions for parameters 
of interest. We calculated posterior probabilities P(β > 0 | data) 
for positive effects and P(β < 0 | data) for negative effects. 

To control for multiple comparisons across 148 cortical regions, 
RBA automatically adjusts inference thresholds. We considered 
effects credible when the posterior probability exceeded 0.95 
(equivalent to a Bayesian analog of p < 0.05, two-tailed). Effect 
sizes were quantified as the predicted change in ITPC for a 1-SD 
increase in spectral exponent.

Convergence was assessed via R̂ < 1.01 for all parameters and 
visual inspection of trace plots. Model fit was evaluated using 
posterior predictive checks

In this model I am more interested in “random” ecect of exponent than ﬁxed

Z-normalizing is useful for interpretation later, particularly when exponent_z is at 0

::: {#bsn2025 fig-scap="Values of exponet of the slope "}
![](figures/chapter4/bsn2025.png){#fig-bsn2025}

Relationship between the slope (parametrized by exponent and the estimated ITPC). Figure on the left: Relationship between Spectral Exponent (z-scored) and ITPC across selected ROIs. Red line indicates linear fit. Data points colored by subject
:::

- Exponent and the offset of the spectrum are different across the brain (Box 1).

- Strong effect of the stimulus (S) on the ITPC (contrast baseline–stimulus), in areas like the auditory regions, but also in temporal lobe, inferior part of primary sensory-motor regions and inferior frontal regions; negative values indicate higher ITPC during stimulation.

- No particular evidence was found for the model *Exponent ~ Stimulus*, namely the stimulation did not influence the exponent per se.

- No significant evidence was found for any of the models involving the Offset either as a predicted variable, and as a predictor, suggesting a marginal role for it in the auditory entrainment.

- Looking for a raw relationship between exponent and ITPC shows a positive relationship between the Exponent and the ITPC, suggesting that higher Exponent is associated with higher ITPC, i.e., higher synchrony during stimulation.

- Hierarchical Bayesian modelling allows to estimate the posterior distribution of the coefficients, which can be used to assess the significance of the effect. It also uses pooling of the data across subjects and regions.  
  The posterior distribution of the coefficient is shown in Box 2, on the right.
